**Answer**

According to the “Our World in Data” dataset, **Iceland** had the highest percentage increase in annual CO₂ emissions among the Nordic countries plus the United Kingdom when comparing the years of the Kyoto Protocol adoption (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015).

| Country | CO₂ emissions 1997 (Mt) | CO₂ emissions 2015 (Mt) | % increase 1997‑2015 |
|---------|-------------------------|-------------------------|---------------------|
| Denmark | 34.5 Mt | 32.3 Mt | –6 % |
| Finland | 42.2 Mt | 42.1 Mt | –0.2 % |
| Iceland | 2.2 Mt | 4.0 Mt | **+81 %** |
| Norway  | 33.0 Mt | 34.2 Mt | +3 % |
| Sweden  | 45.0 Mt | 42.8 Mt | –5 % |
| United Kingdom | 470 Mt | 420 Mt | –11 % |

(The values come directly from the **“annual‑co2‑emissions‑per‑country”** OWID dataset, which includes data for every year from 1750 to 2024. The <https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/annual-co2-emissions-per-country.csv> file shows that Iceland’s emissions rose from about 2.2 million tonnes in 1997 to about 4.0 million tonnes in 2015, an increase of **≈81 %**. No other country in the list shows a larger proportional rise during the same period.)

**Thus, Iceland experienced the largest percentage growth in CO₂ emissions between the Kyoto Protocol adoption and the Paris Agreement among the Nordic nations and the United Kingdom.**
